code.title: Stack objects die in reverse order, heap objects when you say

followUps: Stack overflow happens when the stack runs out of its fixed space, usually from recursion that never stops or a very large local array. Each call needs a frame (locals plus return address); with a typical 8 MB stack and 100-byte frames, about 80,000 nested calls is the limit. A local int big[10000000] (40 MB) overflows immediately. Fix by adding a base case, looping instead of recursing, or putting big data on the heap (std::vector).

The vector object itself (usually 3 pointers, 24 bytes) lives wherever you declare it, but the elements it stores are on the heap. std::vector<int> v(1000) as a local puts 24 bytes on the stack and 4000 bytes on the heap. When v goes out of scope its destructor frees the heap buffer. A std::array<int,1000> is different: all 4000 bytes sit inside the object, so on the stack.

Heap allocation is slower because the allocator has to find a free block of the right size, update its bookkeeping, and often take a lock or touch shared state, costing tens of nanoseconds. A stack allocation is just one subtraction on the stack pointer (about 1 cycle) and the memory is almost certainly already in cache. Heap blocks are also scattered, so later accesses miss the cache more. Example: allocating 1,000,000 small objects with new is often 20 to 50 times slower than using locals or one big vector.

code.title: RAII guard releases on return and on exception

followUps: When an exception is thrown, C++ unwinds the stack and runs the destructor of every fully built automatic object on the way out, so RAII objects release their resources even though the normal code path was skipped. In the program, g2 then g1 are released before the catch block runs. That is why RAII code needs no try/finally: cleanup is written once in the destructor and works on return, break and throw alike.

It can syntactically, but it should not. Destructors are noexcept by default since C++11, so a throw inside one calls std::terminate. The deeper reason: during unwinding for exception A, a second exception B escaping a destructor leaves the runtime with two active exceptions, which it cannot handle. Catch and log errors inside the destructor, and offer an explicit close() that can report failure for callers who care.

Common ones: std::vector, std::string and other containers (memory), std::unique_ptr and std::shared_ptr (heap objects), std::lock_guard, std::unique_lock and std::scoped_lock (mutexes), std::fstream (files), std::jthread (joins on destruction), and std::ofstream flushing on close. Each acquires in its constructor or creator and releases in its destructor, so you never write the cleanup by hand.

code.title: Use-after-free and leak shown with safe alternatives

followUps: The report has three stacks: where the bad access happened (the read or write), where the memory was freed, and where it was originally allocated, plus the address, size of the block and its offset. Example: "READ of size 4 ... freed by thread T0 here ... previously allocated here". Reading the three stacks in order tells you who freed it too early and who still holds the pointer.

Because freed memory is usually still mapped and often still holds the old bytes, so a stale read returns the old, plausible value and nothing crashes. It only breaks when the allocator reuses that block for something else, which depends on timing and load. A test may pass 1000 times and fail in production. ASan avoids this by quarantining freed blocks and marking them poisoned, so any touch is reported immediately.

A direct leak is a block that no pointer anywhere refers to any more: the program lost the only address. An indirect leak is a block still pointed to, but only by other leaked blocks. Example: a leaked linked-list head makes all its nodes indirect leaks. Fixing the direct leak (the head) usually fixes all the indirect ones, so LSan lists direct leaks first.

code.title: unique_ptr: factory, take ownership, borrow

followUps: You only need a virtual destructor in Base if you delete a derived object through a base pointer. A unique_ptr<Base> holding a Derived calls delete on a Base*; without virtual ~Base() that is undefined behaviour and only Base's destructor runs, leaking Derived's members. (A shared_ptr<Base> made from make_shared<Derived> is safe without it, because its deleter remembers the real type.)

release() gives up ownership and returns the raw pointer without deleting it, so you must delete it yourself or hand it to another owner. reset() deletes the current object (and optionally takes a new pointer). Example: p.release() leaves p empty and the object alive; p.reset() leaves p empty and the object destroyed. Ignoring the return value of release() is a classic leak.

Use push_back(std::make_unique<T>(...)) or emplace_back(new ...)-free forms, and std::move for an existing one: v.push_back(std::move(p));. The vector cannot be copied, only moved, but reallocation is fine because the move constructor is noexcept. Reading is by reference: for (auto& p : v), since auto p would try to copy and fail to compile.

code.title: shared_ptr use_count and control block cost

followUps: The deleter is stored in the control block behind a virtual call (type erasure), not in the pointer's type. This lets two shared_ptr<int> with different deleters be the same type and live in the same container, and keeps shared_ptr a fixed two-pointer size. The price is a heap control block and an indirect call at destruction. unique_ptr does the opposite: the deleter is a template parameter, so it is free but part of the type.

Copying costs one atomic increment on the strong count (about 5 to 20 ns uncontended, far worse when many threads hit the same counter) and the destructor costs an atomic decrement. Moving costs nothing atomic: it just steals the two pointers. So pass by const shared_ptr& or by raw reference when you do not need to share ownership, and std::move when handing over a copy you no longer need.

The aliasing constructor makes a shared_ptr that shares ownership (the control block) of one object but points to a different address, such as a member of it. shared_ptr<int> m(owner, &owner->count); keeps the whole owner alive while you use just the int. The use count is shared with owner, so the owner is freed only after both are gone.

code.title: weak_ptr breaks a parent/child cycle

followUps: Because between expired() returning false and lock() being called, another thread can drop the last owner, so the object may be gone when you lock. Always call lock() once and test the result: if (auto sp = w.lock()) { use(*sp); }. The returned shared_ptr then guarantees the object stays alive for the whole block.

lock() does an "increment only if the strong count is not zero" using a compare-and-swap loop: read the count, if it is 0 return empty, otherwise try to swap in count+1 and retry if another thread changed it first. This single atomic step cannot revive an object that is already being destroyed, which a plain load-then-add could.

A weak_ptr is two pointers (16 bytes on 64-bit), like shared_ptr, and it adds one to the weak count in the control block. It does not keep the object alive, but it keeps the control block alive. With make_shared the object and block are one allocation, so the object's raw memory (for example 1 MB) is not returned until the last weak_ptr is gone, even though its destructor already ran.

code.title: shared_ptr cycle leaks; weak_ptr fixes it

followUps: Make the child-to-parent edge weak. The parent owns its children (shared_ptr or unique_ptr downward) and each child holds only a weak_ptr or raw pointer upward. Ownership then forms a tree with no loops, so when the root is released everything below frees. In a doubly linked list the same rule applies: next owns, prev is weak.

When the target provably outlives the holder and you want zero cost: a child that is always destroyed before its parent, a node in an arena where all nodes die together, or hot paths where lock()'s atomic is too expensive. The trade-off is that a raw pointer cannot detect that the object died, so a lifetime bug becomes a silent dangling pointer instead of an empty lock().

Keep an instance counter incremented in constructors and decremented in destructors, then assert it is 0 after a scope that builds and drops the structure (as in the program). Also run the same tests under AddressSanitizer with LeakSanitizer in CI; shared_ptr cycles appear there as indirect leaks. Failing the build on a nonzero count catches regressions the moment someone adds a strong back edge.

code.title: make_unique, make_shared and why they are safer

followUps: In f(std::shared_ptr<A>(new A), g()) the compiler could run new A, then g(), and only then construct the shared_ptr. If g() throws in between, the raw pointer from new has no owner and A leaks. make_shared does allocation and ownership in one function call, so nothing can be interleaved between them.

C++17 says each function argument is evaluated completely before the next one starts (they may still be evaluated in any order, but not interleaved). So shared_ptr<A>(new A) finishes constructing the owner before g() runs, and the old leak is gone. The other benefits of make_shared (one allocation, no naked new) remain.

code.title: Custom deleter wraps a C-style handle

followUps: No for unique_ptr: the default destructor skips the deleter when the stored pointer is null, so a deleter like fclose never sees nullptr. For shared_ptr, constructing one with a null pointer and a custom deleter does still call the deleter on that null when the last owner goes, so the deleter must tolerate null. Guarding with if (f) in the deleter is the safe habit.

unique_ptr needs a pointer type, so give the deleter a nested using pointer = int; (the invalid value must compare equal to nullptr-like zero) or, simpler, write a small RAII class that stores the int and closes it in the destructor, as in the program. Note that a file descriptor 0 is valid, so be careful about what counts as empty.

std::out_ptr and std::inout_ptr adapt a smart pointer to C APIs that return a resource through a T** out-parameter. Example: lib_open(&raw) becomes lib_open(std::out_ptr(smart)). When the call returns, the adaptor stores the pointer in the smart pointer with its deleter, so there is no window where a raw pointer is unowned.

code.title: enable_shared_from_this shares one control block

followUps: Capture strongly (shared_from_this()) when the callback must keep the object alive until it runs, such as a network write that must finish. Capture weakly (weak_from_this() and lock() inside) when the callback should run only if the object still exists, such as a UI update or a timer. A strong capture stored inside the object itself creates a cycle and a leak; weak capture avoids it.

The base class enable_shared_from_this<T> holds a weak_ptr<T>. When a shared_ptr<T> is created for the object (by make_shared or the constructor), the library detects the base and stores a weak reference to that new control block. shared_from_this() just locks that weak_ptr. If no shared_ptr ever owned the object, the weak_ptr is empty and it throws bad_weak_ptr.

code.title: A minimal unique_ptr with move-only ownership

followUps: Because std::vector grows by moving elements only if the move constructor is noexcept; otherwise it copies (to keep its strong guarantee if a move throws). For a move-only type, no copy exists, so it may refuse to move or fall back to a slow path. A throwing move also makes your own code harder to make exception safe. Pointer swaps cannot throw, so mark them noexcept.

Store the deleter as a member only if it has state. The standard approach is to inherit from the deleter (empty base optimisation) or mark the member [[no_unique_address]] (C++20); either way an empty functor adds 0 bytes, so sizeof(unique_ptr<T>) stays 8. A function-pointer or capturing-lambda deleter holds real data, so it makes the object 16 bytes or more.

With an incomplete type (pimpl: std::unique_ptr<Impl> impl; in a header where Impl is only forward declared), the destructor must see the complete type because it calls delete. So declare ~Widget(); in the header and define it (even as = default) in the .cpp where Impl is complete; same for move operations. Otherwise you get a compile error about an incomplete type in default_delete.

code.title: Atomic reference counting with safe lock()

followUps: Because another thread can drop the strong count to 0 and destroy the object between your load and your increment, so you would raise 0 to 1 and hand out a pointer to a destroyed object. Example: thread A loads 1, thread B releases the last owner (count 0, object destroyed), A stores 2. The compare-and-swap loop fails when the value changed, and rereads it, seeing 0 and giving up.

std::atomic<std::shared_ptr<T>> (C++20) makes the shared_ptr variable itself safe to load, store and compare-exchange from many threads. A plain shared_ptr is only safe to copy as separate objects: two threads reading and writing the same variable is a data race on the two pointers. Typical use: publish a new immutable config snapshot while readers atomically load the current one.

libstdc++ checks whether the program is linked with threads (via __gthread_active_p) and, if not, uses plain increments instead of atomic ones in the control block. Single-threaded programs then avoid the cost of locked instructions. It is a policy choice of the library, not part of the standard, and it can surprise you if a thread is started later by a plugin.

code.title: Leak hunt: counting live objects over time

followUps: Watch whether memory keeps growing after the workload is steady and stays high after load stops. A true leak grows linearly with the number of operations and heap profiler snapshots show the same stack gaining bytes. Fragmentation or a cache that stops growing levels off, and allocator stats show large "free but not returned" space. Calling malloc_trim or checking jemalloc "allocated vs resident" separates them: if allocated is flat but resident is high, it is fragmentation.

An indirect leak is memory that is still referenced, but only from other leaked memory, so no live variable can reach it. Example: a leaked tree root (direct leak) holds 1,000 child nodes (indirect leaks). In LSan output the direct leak is the root cause to fix; the indirect entries are consequences. A shared_ptr cycle typically shows up as indirect, since each member points to the next.

Write a test that runs the operation 10,000 times in a loop and asserts the live-object count (as in the program) or the process's memory returns to a baseline plus a small tolerance. Also run the unit tests under ASan/LSan in CI so any true leak fails the job. For example: after 10,000 requests, assert(live["cached"] <= cacheLimit).

code.title: Choosing the right pointer: reference, raw, unique, shared, weak

followUps: Because shared ownership makes lifetime unclear: nobody knows who will destroy the object or when, destruction order becomes unpredictable, cycles can leak, and every copy costs an atomic operation. It often hides a missing design decision about who owns what. Prefer unique_ptr with borrowed references, and use shared_ptr only when several owners really have independent lifetimes, such as async callbacks.

Yes to the first: std::shared_ptr<T> s = std::move(u); works and is a common way to relax ownership later. No to the reverse: once several owners exist, no single one may take sole ownership, so there is no conversion from shared_ptr to unique_ptr. Return unique_ptr from factories, since the caller can always upgrade it to a shared_ptr for free.
